text: Every program is told what to do in two ways when it starts: by the words typed after its name, and by settings left waiting for it in its environment. Almost no program writes down what it accepts in either.

heading: A typo that says nothing
text:
Misspell an option and you may get an error. Misspell an environment setting and you get silence - always. No warning, no failure: only a program quietly doing the wrong thing, found out days later.

Ask which settings a program really accepts, and the honest answer is: read its source code. The table in its documentation was typed by hand, and it drifted the day somebody forgot to update it.

heading: One declaration, two doors
text:
With argenv a program declares each of its inputs once: its name, its kind, the values it allows, its default, what it is for. That one declaration is what the program itself reads - so it cannot drift from the truth.

And an option on the command line and a setting in the environment stop being two things. They are **one setting with two doors**, so they share a kind, a default and a description.

heading: A socket with a label
text: A wall socket says what it gives: this voltage, this shape of plug. You do not find out by plugging something in and watching what burns.

heading: Written down, so it can be checked
text:
Because the list is published as a plain document, a tool can check any way of starting the program against it before the program runs - and say: this setting is not known; did you mean that one?

That works for a program written in any language, even one that never used argenv, as long as somebody wrote its list down.

heading: What it does not cover
text: It covers what the operating system hands a program at its start - not configuration files, which mostly have their own descriptions already. And a contract helps only where someone publishes it.

heading: Where it stands
text: Published as a Rust library, and used by a real tool. Two questions of its design are still open.
An agent can write a program in minutes and still be unable to try it: the moment the program asks for a key press or draws a screen, the agent is outside, looking at a closed door.

heading: Tools made for hands and eyes
text: Interactive tools - pickers, menus, editors, whole graphical programs - are made for a person at a keyboard. An agent that built one cannot check it works; an agent that needs one cannot use it. So a person is called in to press keys and read the screen, mid-task, by hand.

heading: Two doors, and a driver
text: Every tool keeps **two doors**: the interactive one for people, and a structured one - plain arguments, output a program can read - for agents and scripts. Most of the time an agent walks through the second.\n\nFor checking the first door itself, a **terminal driver** starts the program, presses keys, waits until the screen shows what it should, and reads the screen as text. Interactions written down as **scenes** - press this, expect that - run on every change, and their screens become evidence.

heading: A ramp beside the stairs
text: A building with a ramp beside its stairs is not a different building. Everyone can enter; each by the way that suits them.

heading: Called, not copied
text: Like the package conveyor, it is called: a project declares its scenes and calls the conveyor at a pinned version. The same driver is offered to agents over the Model Context Protocol, the open standard through which programs such as Blender and Photoshop already open themselves to agents.

heading: What it does not do yet
text: Graphical programs come later, through Linux's accessibility interface or each program's own connector. A scene proves what it was written to expect, and no more.

heading: Where it stands
text: Researched and planned; nothing built. It follows two heavier pieces of work and then begins with the driver, tried first on ocoeco's own picker - the tool whose real-terminal check could not be made.
Ask someone why their project exists and how it will get there, and you will usually get two different answers on two different days - and a third from their colleague.

heading: Carried in people's heads
text: Most work runs on what a few people remember: why we started, what done means, which steps really matter, how we know one is finished. When they are busy, or gone, the work goes on by habit - and nobody can say any more whether it is still heading where it meant to.

heading: Four questions, each leading to the next
text:
Essence is a way of writing down the heart of any process as four answers.

**Why does this exist?** - told for someone who knows nothing about it. **What must it reach?** - as steps nobody could argue about, because each names its evidence. **How is each step delivered and proven?** - what actually does it, and why we care. **What is happening now?** - produced by the work itself, not written about it afterwards.

The four are a chain. What happens should serve a step; a step should serve the idea. Whatever serves nothing is noise. Whatever nothing serves is a wish.

heading: Like a recipe someone else can cook from
text: A cook's own notes say: the usual, until it looks right. A recipe says what the dish is for, what it should become, each step, and how to tell that the step is done. The notes work only for the cook.

heading: Seen, not only read
text: Written this way, a project can be drawn: its reason, its path, what carries each step, and its pulse - on one page. And the gaps show themselves. A step with nothing delivering it stands empty. That is the point.

heading: What it will not do
text: It does not make the work good. It shows whether the work knows what it is for. And it asks for an honesty the method cannot enforce: evidence can be chosen badly.

heading: Where it stands
text: The method is written, and this project describes itself with it. The observatory draws a project's whole chain on one page; the measure of how completely each project tells its essence is being built.
An AI agent can write code all day. What it cannot do, from inside a chat window, is touch your machine: run the build, flash the phone, see whether it worked.

heading: Hands, or blind trust
text: The usual answers are both bad. Copy commands back and forth by hand, and the person becomes the agent's hands. Or give the agent a remote shell and hope - with no record of what it did, and no way to say: stop.

heading: A desk between the agent and the machine
text:
lab-agent is that desk. The agent hands over a job; the machine runs it; the result comes back.

Everything passes through a place both can see. What is being done now is on a board. What was done is kept. And the person can write to the agent, and be answered, without stopping the work.

heading: A workshop's job tickets
text: Each ticket says what was asked, who took it, and what came of it. Nobody has to remember. Anybody can look.

heading: What it is not
text: It is not a cage: it trusts the agent with the machine it serves. It is a way of working in the open. And it serves one lab machine today.

heading: Where it stands
text: In daily use: every build, test and flash of these projects passes through it. It shows a board, carries messages both ways, and tells any agent the ways of working before it starts.
A spreadsheet is easy to change and impossible to review. Alter one cell, and afterwards nobody can see what was changed, by whom, or why.

heading: Safe and locked away, or open and unreliable
text: Keep a project's facts in a database and they are safe - and locked away: nobody sees a change go by, nobody reviews it. Keep them in documents and anyone can edit them - and within a month they contradict each other.

heading: Tables, kept as plain text
text:
tad - text as data - keeps each table as a plain text file, one line for each row, in the same place as the code. So a change to a fact is a change to one line: it can be read, reviewed, discussed and undone like any other change.

A guard stands at the door. Whatever is edited is loaded, checked against the rules the data must obey, and written back in one fixed form. Anything else is refused.

heading: A ledger, not a whiteboard
text: On a whiteboard the latest hand wins and the past is wiped away. In a ledger every entry stays, in order, with its author.

heading: Pages drawn from the data
text: The pages people read are drawn from the tables. So a page cannot say something the data does not.

heading: What it is for, and not
text: It suits facts that people decide and review - hundreds or thousands of rows, not millions. And it began as a set of scripts.

heading: Where it stands
text: Working, and in use by several repositories. It is kept as it is: what it taught lives on in ocoeco, where the new work goes.

When your program uses someone else's code, you do not really have that code. You have a promise that a registry will hand you something by that name - and a hope that nobody changes what the name means.

heading: Borrowed, not owned
text:
A dependency you cannot change is a risk you cannot manage. Find a bug in it and you have two bad choices: wait for a stranger to fix it, or copy the code into your own project and look after that private copy for ever, as it drifts further from the original every month.

And a fix you do make is trapped where you made it. Getting it back to the people who could use it means untangling it from everything else you changed.

heading: A cutting, not a copy
text: Rhizoid makes each dependency a real fork that you own - a **rhizoid-cutting**, or rhizcut. It is pinned to an exact state, so nothing moves under you. It follows the original when you choose, not when someone else decides. You can patch it today, without anyone's permission. And when your patch is good, it goes home as one clean change, with none of your local history attached.

heading: Like a gardener's cutting
text: A cutting is a living piece of the parent plant. It grows in your soil and you prune it as you need - and it is still the same plant, so what you learn from it can go back to the garden it came from.

heading: Nothing hidden
text: There is no central list to trust and no lock file only a tool can read. Each cutting carries its own small note saying where it came from and what state it holds. And the tool tells you when a cutting has drifted from what you declared - it does not merely repeat the declaration back to you.

heading: What it does not fix
text: Rhizoid works in the world as it is: files, git, forks. It does not cure the deeper trouble - that software is identified by name. That is Rhizome's work, and a much longer road. Rhizoid is what can be used while that road is walked.

heading: Where it stands
text: Its commands are settled and the layer that reads its declarations is built and tested. The commands themselves are being written.

Writing a useful program is half the work. The other half is getting it onto someone's computer - built for their machine, signed so they can trust it, kept up to date - and that half is usually done badly, or copied from the last project and done badly again.

heading: The same five hundred lines, again
text: Two of our own tools carry nearly identical delivery machinery: cut a release, build it for two kinds of processor, prove where it was built, install it on six systems to see it works, and publish a signed package repository. Each copy drifts. A fix made in one never reaches the other. And the next project starts by copying the newest one - including its mistakes.

heading: One conveyor, called, not copied
text: The conveyor does the delivering once, for everyone. A project keeps one short declaration - its name, how its releases are named, which systems it ships to, which key signs it - and calls the conveyor at a pinned version. Improving the conveyor improves every project that moves to the new version, and none of them is changed by surprise.

heading: Like a postal service
text: Nobody builds their own mail van to send a letter. You write the address clearly and hand it over; the service knows the roads.

heading: What the machines actually run
text: It ships what our machines use: Arch Linux packages for the lab and desktops, Alpine packages for postmarketOS phones - from one declaration, each with a signed repository. Other systems join when someone needs them.

heading: What it does not do
text: It does not decide when a project releases or what its version is: that stays with each language's own tool. It cannot make a broken program work - it can only refuse to publish one that fails its checks.

heading: Where it stands
text: Designed, from the delivery machinery of snapall and lab-agent. The first step is to move both onto it with nothing visible changing for anyone who installed them; then Alpine packages, and the phone's shell as their first user.

Your phone is the most personal computer you own, and the one you control least. You cannot see what it runs. You cannot change it. And when its maker stops sending updates - usually after a few years - a machine that works perfectly well becomes a risk you carry in your pocket.

heading: Two doors, both locked
text:
Almost every phone in the world runs one of two systems, each owned by one company. The hardware underneath could run something else: Linux, the free system that already runs most of the world's servers.

But a phone that runs Linux today can rarely be someone's only phone. The call drops, the camera stays dark, the battery does not last the day. And every phone model needs its own patient work, done by a handful of volunteers, mostly started again from nothing for each device.

heading: Make the work ordinary, and make the truth visible
text:
Two things, together.

**A conveyor.** A lab of tools and written procedures, so that bringing Linux to a phone is the same known steps every time - flash it, check it, listen to it, fix what fails, send the fix where everyone gets it - done by a person or by an agent, and never leaving the phone broken.

**An honest picture.** Every thing a phone must do, set against every system that could do it: what works, what half works, what is missing - and, shown plainly, what nobody has measured yet.

heading: A workshop, not a miracle
text: One brilliant mechanic can fix one car. A workshop with the right lifts and gauges and written procedures fixes any car - and the next mechanic starts where the last one stopped.

heading: As good as Android - and counted
text: The aim is plain: a phone running Linux that an ordinary person could use as their only phone, and not feel they gave something up. We count towards it one feature at a time, and a feature counts only when something has shown that it works.

heading: What is still hard
text: Some parts of a phone are kept shut by their makers - the modem, the camera, the secure chip - and can only be worked with from outside. Banking and payments depend on decisions that are not ours. There is one phone in the lab so far. And for Linux phones as a whole, most of the picture still reads: not known yet.

heading: Where it stands
text: One phone, a Xiaomi POCO X3 NFC, sits in the lab. It can be flashed to a known state by one command, and it is checked after every start. Sound plays from both of its speakers. Its microphone and its calls are still ahead. The picture lists forty-six things a phone does, across seven systems.
Working on the inside of a phone is like repairing a watch you cannot open: every step is slow, and one slip leaves it dead on the table.

heading: Every phone, the same pain again
text: People who bring Linux to phones each keep their own scripts, their own notes, their own superstitions. What one learned about not stranding a device, the next learns again - on their own device.

heading: One lab for any phone
text:
devlab is the lab's set of tools. It reaches a phone however it can be reached, flashes it to a known state, sets up a fresh one, checks it after every start, listens to its speakers, and tries a risky change once, in a way that falls back by itself.

What differs between phones is written on one sheet - the device's manifest. The tools stay the same.

heading: A pilot's checklist
text: Not because pilots are forgetful. Because the cost of one skipped step is too high to leave to memory.

heading: What it has not reached
text: One phone has been through it so far. Tests that need a human hand or eye are not built in yet. And it runs from a lab machine, not from a pocket.

heading: Where it stands
text: Today it flashes, sets up, checks, watches, listens to and tries test kernels on one phone.

This is one particular phone - a Xiaomi POCO X3 NFC, known by its codename surya - kept on a desk and plugged into a lab machine, so that making Linux work on it can be done carefully, the same way each time, and without ever leaving it broken.

heading: A phone is easy to strand
text: Work on a phone's deepest parts and one wrong step leaves it dark, with nobody near to press its buttons. So people work cautiously and slowly, keep their fixes in their heads, and lose them at the next clean start.

heading: Everything about this phone, written down
text:
The lab holds what is true of this phone and nothing else: how to reach it, what to bake into every fresh start, which checks it must pass, which tones a microphone should hear from it. The tools are the same for any phone; this is the one sheet that makes them fit this one.

Every experiment is a single try that falls back by itself. The phone always returns to a state known to work.

heading: A patient's chart at the end of the bed
text: Whoever comes next - a person or an agent - reads the chart and knows what was done, what holds, and what must not be touched without care.

heading: What it has not reached
text: Its microphone does not work yet, and no call has been made on it. Its cameras, its fingerprint reader and its NFC have not been tried.

heading: Where it stands
text: It can be flashed to a known state by one command. Twenty-two checks pass after every start. Sound plays from both speakers; a machine hearing it reliably still waits for a microphone fixed in place.
The trouble with keeping records about work is that keeping them is more work. So they are kept late, kept wrong, or not kept at all.

heading: Data made by work
text:
ocoeco begins from one rule: a project's data should be produced by its work - its commits, its builds, its tests, its releases - not typed up afterwards.

What only a person can supply - a plan, a decision, a judgment - is written once, where the work happens, and never copied anywhere else.

heading: A ship's log, kept by the ship
text: The engine counts its own hours. The instruments record the weather. Only the captain's decisions are written by hand. Nobody rebuilds the voyage from memory once the ship is in port.

heading: One language, so the pieces join
text:
It is a small set of agreements. Plain text tables that anyone can read and that show exactly what changed. A mark by which a repository says: I am part of this. Shared names for the common things - the idea, the path, how it works, what was done. And a way for one project's data to feed another's, every line carrying where it came from.

A project joins with one command, and can check, before it publishes anything, that it will be read.

heading: What it cannot gather
text: It can gather what happened. It cannot gather what nobody recorded and no tool observed. So its real work is turning more of what matters into something the work itself produces.

heading: Where it stands
text: Working. It finds marked projects, gathers their activity, releases and test results every day, and reads their tables into the observatory. Still ahead: travelling into every repository as an owned part rather than a copy.
Data about a project, however true, is a pile of lines until someone can look at it and understand.

heading: Pictures made for insiders
text: Most pictures of projects are drawn for the people already inside them: charts of whatever was easy to count, in words you must already know. Each project draws itself its own way - and, naturally, in its best light.

heading: One eye for every project
text:
ocoeco-engine takes what projects say about themselves and draws it the same way for all of them: a page that shows why a project exists, what it must reach, how each step is delivered and proven, and what is happening now.

No project designs its own page. None can look better than its evidence.

heading: Like the legend of a map
text: On a good map a river is always the same blue and a road always the same line. Learn the legend once, and you can read any country.

heading: Plain pages, anyone's lens, any language
text: It makes plain web pages: no scripts, nothing that tracks you, readable on a phone or on paper. A family of projects is seen through a lens, which anyone may declare as one small file. And every word of the interface lives in a catalog, so the same site exists in each language.

heading: What it cannot do
text: It draws what it is given, and no more. It knows only a few kinds of view. And it is redrawn every few hours, not the moment something changes.

heading: Where it stands
text: Running: it draws this site in English and Russian - every project's essence, and three grand views.

Ask of any project: how close is it to working? To being as good as it should be? What is being done right now, and why? Usually the answer lives in someone's head - or in a document that stopped being true months ago.

heading: Pictures that go stale
text: A status page is written by hand, so it describes the day it was written. A dashboard shows whatever was easy to count. Neither can tell you whether it is still true. And across many projects, made by many people, nobody can see the whole at all.

heading: Let each project say what is true of itself
text:
Every project keeps its own state as plain data, in its own repository: why it exists, the path it is on, what proves each step, what was done and what was turned down. A small mark makes it findable.

The observatory finds every marked project, gathers what they share, and draws one living picture. Nothing is copied by hand - so nothing can quietly drift away from the truth.

heading: Like a weather map
text: Nobody draws a weather map from memory. Stations report what they measure, and the map is whatever the stations say now. Here, every project is a station.

heading: Honest by construction
text:
What has not been measured is shown as not known - never as failure. What is planned and not yet begun is shown calm, not in the red of broken things. A step counts as reached only when the evidence for it exists.

And anyone may look through a lens of their own: a grand view of any family of projects is itself just a small repository, which the observatory finds and draws like its own.

heading: What it cannot do
text: It shows what projects say about themselves. It cannot make a project honest, and it cannot notice a problem that nobody measured. A picture is not the work.

heading: Where it stands
text: Running. It finds its projects, gathers their data every few hours, and publishes this site in two languages. Every view you are looking at is drawn from the projects' own records.

Every piece of software you have ever tried to build came with a list: install these fourteen things first. **That list is an apology.** The machine that built the program knew exactly what it needed, down to the last piece - and that knowledge was thrown away, and a paragraph of instructions written in its place, asking you to rebuild it from memory and guesswork.

heading: What went wrong, a long time ago
text:
We call a piece of software by a name someone chose, and then treat the name as the thing. Rename it or move it, and everything that pointed at it breaks. We say two parts are compatible by comparing version numbers on whole components, when the truth lives in which few functions each part actually touches. And we seal everything into boxes - files, packages, programs - and then spend a great part of our working lives making the boxes fit.

Nobody designed this. Early computers read one file at a time from a reel of tape, so the file became the unit of everything, and sixty years of tools were built on top of that accident.

heading: Imagine your identity were your address
text: Move house and you become, legally, a different person. Everyone who knew you must be told, one by one, or they lose you for ever. We would call that an absurd way to run a society. It is exactly how we run software.

heading: Identify things by what they are
text:
Give every small piece of software a fingerprint, computed from its own contents and from the fingerprints of everything it relies on. Now a thing is the same thing wherever it lives and whatever it is called - and a different thing is different, however alike the name. Names stay, as labels anyone may change. Nothing depends on them any more.

Almost everything else follows without being designed. There are no versions to clash, because you hold exact things. There are no copies, because two identical things were never two. There is nothing to install, because what a program needs is known exactly and arrives the moment it is touched. And when you change one line deep inside someone else's work, you get your own version of that one piece - while theirs, and everyone who uses it, stays exactly as it was.

heading: Sam wants the chime to stop
text:
Sam is a nurse, not a programmer. On night shifts their messaging app chimes for every message, and it has no setting to chime only for the ward. Today that is not difficult - it is impossible: the code that decides it is public, and might as well be on the moon.

Here Sam types **notification sound**, sees the very thing that decides it, and finds that eleven thousand people already use a version that chimes only for chosen groups. Two clicks. Sam did not become a developer. Sam changed a setting that happened to sit one step deeper than the settings screen goes.

heading: One move, repeated
text:
Which version is this? What does it need? Does it need rebuilding? Do these two conflict? Who is affected by this flaw? Is that advice still true? Today every one of these is a guess, and each guess costs an ocean of human hours. Here every one is a calculation.

That is the whole idea: **replace a guess with a calculation.** Everything else is engineering.

heading: What is still hard
text:
Nothing here needs inventing: each part already runs somewhere, built by people solving other problems. The danger is not the engineering. It is that the first person to use it must come out ahead on the very first day, alone - or nobody ever will.

And some things stay human. Someone still has to notice the bug. Someone still has to explain why.

heading: Where it stands
text:
The idea is written down whole, and its first step is planned: a small tool, Hypha, that reads real code, fingerprints every piece, and proves a piece can be lifted out and still run. Nothing is built yet. It is kept ready at the edge of our other work - which runs into the old ways a little more every day.

The full text is the manifesto in this project's repository: **Stop managing software. Start growing it.**
